blocks.text: Have you ever wondered how numbers are built and why some numbers are called 'prime'? Let's explore the world of whole numbers and primes!

blocks.markdown: Whole numbers are the set of numbers that include zero and all positive numbers without fractions or decimals. Examples are 0, 1, 2, 3, etc. Understanding whole numbers is fundamental to mastering arithmetic operations.

blocks.title: Whole Numbers
blocks.text: Whole numbers are non-negative numbers without fractions or decimals, starting from zero.

blocks.markdown: Prime numbers are special whole numbers greater than 1 that have no divisors other than 1 and themselves. For example, 2, 3, 5, and 7 are prime numbers. They are the building blocks of all numbers.

blocks.title: Finding Prime Factors

steps.text: Start by dividing 56 by the smallest prime number, which is 2.
Continue dividing by 2 until you cannot divide evenly.
Now, 7 is a prime number. So, the prime factors of 56 are 2, 2, 2, and 7.

blocks.answer: The prime factors of 56 are 2, 2, 2, and 7.

blocks.markdown: Let's practice the basic arithmetic operations using whole numbers. Remember, addition and multiplication are commutative, meaning the order does not matter, but subtraction and division are not.

blocks.title: Exam Tip
blocks.text: Always check your calculations twice, especially with subtraction and division, to avoid simple errors.

Basic operations on whole numbers include addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
